newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE pledges support after deal on Albania poll.
newsitem.headline: OSCE pledges support after deal on Albania poll.

text.p: European mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday Albanian politicians had agreed to go ahead with a general election on June 29, ending days of deadlock that had threatened to plunge the Balkan state into further crisis.

Vranitzky, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) envoy to Albania since widespread violence erupted there in March, pledged that the international community would now do all it could to help prepare the two-round election and ensure it was free and fair.

"(Albanian) Prime Minister (Bashkim) Fino called me last night and he told me the political parties had agreed to solve the political situation in Albania...They have confirmed the election will be held on June 29," Vranitzky said.

Speaking at a news conference after addressing the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council, the former Austrian chancellor said a number of sticking points had been resolved, including the makeup of central and regional electoral commissions.

He said President Sali Berisha, whose rightist Democratic Party won a huge majority in a disputed election a year ago, had handed his power to nominate the heads of the commissions to Fino, a member of the main opposition Socialist Party.

The Socialists, reformed heirs of the former communist party which ruled Albania for more than 40 years until 1991, boycotted the first round of a general election on May 26 last year, complaining the Democrats were not allowing opposition parties access to the commissions or the voting counts.

The concession by Berisha, in power since 1992, is a significant one and should calm any unease among the opposition that the dominant Democrats would try to instal party backers as commission heads, as was largely the case last year.

Fino became prime minister in March when a national unity government was set up aimed at preventing further anarchy in the former Stalinist state. Violence and looting broke out after weeks of protest by impoverished Albanians who lost their savings in pyramid investment schemes.
The parties cleared up one major stumbling block and finally agreed to the election of 115 parliamentary seats by majority voting and 40 through proportional representation.

Vranitzky said all parties had also agreed to equal access to the media. Opposition parties last year complained that state-run television and radio were controlled by the Democrats and that they did not receive the same airtime.
Vranitzky said the 54-nation OSCE would give full support to help organise the election and would send as many observers as was deemed necessary with the Council of Europe.

"We will help Albania. The whole international community is speaking with unanimity. There are no dissenting voices," he added. He went on to urge all OSCE member states quickly to provide the resources necessary but declined to put a figure on the number of OSCE observers to be sent to Albania.

The OSCE last year produced a highly critical election report. Observers of the security forum catalogued a range of poll irregularities, including incomplete electoral registers, ballot stuffing and voter intimidation.
The Council of Europe, set up after World War Two to monitor human rights and democracy, produced a milder report.
Vranitzky said the differing reports produced a controversial situation in Albania, with one side using the OSCE to back their claims, the other the Council of Europe.
Vranitkzy said he had visited parliamentarians of the Council of Europe in Strasbourg and they had agreed that they would compile a common report following the June 29 poll.
